title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E449 develops power residues modulo a prime P, assuming a primitive root a exists. In §57 (previous page), with P = 2n+1, the quadratic residues are the even powers 1, a^2, a^4, …. Since a^n ≡ −1, it follows that −1 is a quadratic residue iff n is even, i.e. iff P ≡ 1 (mod 4).

Coroll. 1 (§58): for primes P = 4n+1, −1 ≡ 4n is a residue. Because residues are closed under multiplication, α residue implies −α residue: the 'complement' P−α of every residue is a residue.

Coroll. 2 (§59): for primes P = 4n−1, −1 is a non-residue. Since residue × non-residue = non-residue, the complement of every residue is a non-residue.

Theorem (§60): for a prime p = 4n+1 one can always find a sum of two squares, each prime to p, that is divisible by p, and one square may be chosen arbitrarily.

Proof: take any b with p ∤ b, and let b^2 ≡ β. By §58, −β is a residue, so some x has x^2 ≡ −β. Then p | b^2 + x^2, and neither square is divisible by p.

Next page: x may be reduced to |x| < p/2. This gives n relations 1+p'^2, 4+q^2, … all divisible by p, with quotient below 2n+2. These relations prepare a descent proof of Fermat's two-squares theorem.
errors: No errors in the page's own reasoning. It depends on the existence of a primitive root (used in §57 for a^n ≡ −1). Euler's argument for that existence in this memoir is generally regarded as incomplete; Gauss (Disquisitiones, art. 56) criticized earlier attempts. So the page's results are only as rigorous as that foundation, though each can be proved independently (e.g. via Euler's criterion or Wilson's theorem).
The theorem should require b not divisible by p. This is implicit in 'ad eum primorum' and is stated at the end of the proof.

ideas.what: −1 is a quadratic residue mod p iff p ≡ 1 mod 4 (first supplementary law), derived via a primitive root
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (also Fermat implicitly; Lagrange gave a proof via Wilson's theorem)
ideas.where_published: Euler E262 and E241 (sums of two squares), E552, and here in E449

ideas.what: Multiplicativity of residues and non-residues (R·R = R, R·N = N), so the complement of a residue is a residue iff p ≡ 1 mod 4
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E262 and Opuscula analytica), formalized by Legendre and Gauss
ideas.where_published: E262 'Theoremata circa residua ex divisione potestatum relicta'; E449

ideas.what: For p ≡ 1 mod 4 and any b prime to p there is x with p | b^2 + x^2, x < p/2; a step toward the two-squares theorem
ideas.modern_name: Solvability of x^2 ≡ −b^2 (mod p); lemma for Fermat's two-squares theorem via descent
ideas.where_published: E241 'Demonstratio theorematis Fermatiani omnem numerum primum formae 4n+1 esse summam duorum quadratorum'

deep.surprise_reason: Standard, well-documented material: the first supplementary law and the lemma preparing Euler's descent proof of the two-squares theorem. Euler published all of this elsewhere, and E449 itself is well known.
